sweep_summary: Three target items. (1) Good 2004 Lingua (the catalog's deciding source) re-downloaded from the author's page — byte-identical to the catalog copy — and re-read: split lexicon, tonal classes with no stress, pitch accent class with stress derived from the leftmost H by trochaic parsing; catalog quote verbatim; confirms. (2) Good 'A twice-mixed creole?' (Glottolog 2006 ms = Studies in Language 33, 2009; listed by Glottolog as a dictionary is a Glottolog mis-typing) already held by the project as the author preprint; historical paper restating the same analysis (stress in pitch-accented words predictable from accent position; tonal words unmarked for accent); confirms. (3) Rountree 1994 Missiology is an ethnographic piece on proverbs/wisdom literature — not relevant, paywalled SAGE DOI, priority none. Beyond the list: the primary source of the catalog's stress rule, Rountree 1972b 'The phonological structure of stems in Saramaccan' (Grimes ed., Languages of the Guianas, SIL 1972, pp. 22-27), was located as an open Rosetta Project scan on archive.org and read first-hand; its pp. 25-26 stress rule (first long syllable of the foot, else penult of the foot; leftmost stress heaviest; disyllabic LH stems vary) matches Good's block quote exactly, so the catalog locator can cite Rountree 1972b: 25-26 directly instead of 'as quoted by Good'. Good 2005 (J. Portuguese Linguistics, held by the project) gives the crispest formulation of the stress-from-accent algorithm (p. 11). catalog's classification 'tonal' / tonal-OR-pitch accent stands; nothing read contradicts it. Only unread candidate: McWhorter & Good 2012 grammar ch. 2 'Prosodic phonology' (De Gruyter, paywalled, priority low — same co-author, expected to restate Good 2004). all look-ups went through Crossref/Glottolog/archive.org downloads. new_statements.quote: The stress pattern of stems can be predicted according to the following rules. (1) The first long syllable in each foot of the stem is stressed. (2) If there is no long syllable, the next to the last syllable in the phonological foot is stressed. In simple stems that correspond to more than one phonological foot, the first stress is the heaviest. Compound stems remain to be investigated. Two-syllable stems with a LH tone pattern have no set pattern; the stress varies freely between the syllables: 'bebe ~ be'be 'drink', 'guli ~ gu'li 'swallow', 'kini ~ ki'ni 'knee'.
new_statements.citation: Rountree, S. Catherine. 1972. The phonological structure of stems in Saramaccan. In Joseph E. Grimes (ed.), Languages of the Guianas (SIL Publications in Linguistics 35), 22-27. Norman: SIL / University of Oklahoma.
new_statements.reading: First-hand SIL field description (1968-69, Upper Suriname River dialect). Tone: 'Every vowel carries one tone. Two tones, high and low, are contrastive' (p. 25). Stress: predictable within the phonological foot — the first long (VV/diphthong) syllable of the foot, otherwise the penult of the foot; in multi-foot stems the first (leftmost) stress is strongest; disyllabic LH stems have free variation. This is the very passage the catalog currently holds only second-hand, as Good 2004's block quote (preprint p. 14); the first-hand text matches it. It supports the catalog's 'tonal' coding (tone is the lexical contrast; stress is a non-contrastive, derived property) and does not overturn Good 2004's reanalysis, in which stress exists only in the pitch accent class and follows from the leftmost H/accent (Good 2004 preprint p. 18: 'word stress can be predicted from the location of the leftmost high-tone TBU').

new_statements.quote: C'est la seule langue creole connue jusqu'a l'heure actuelle dans laquelle le ton est nettement distinctif. [...] le systeme complique qui comprend deux niveaux de ton, trois contours de ton et la duree des voyelles peut s'analyser comme un systeme de deux niveaux de tons (aigu et grave) relativement tres simple, dans lequel chaque syllabe ou mot doit porter un niveau du ton. [fn. 2:] Nous ne parlerons pas ici en detail de la difference entre une langue tonale (Saramaccan) et une langue a accent (Sranan). [...] En Saramaccan, la syllabe est porteuse de la hauteur tonale [...], tandis qu'en Sranan c'est le mot qui est porteur d'une difference de hauteur tonale.
new_statements.translation: It is the only creole language known to date in which tone is clearly distinctive. [...] the complicated system comprising two tone levels, three tone contours and vowel length can be analysed as a relatively very simple system of two tone levels (high and low), in which every syllable or word must carry a tone level. [fn. 2:] We will not discuss here in detail the difference between a tone language (Saramaccan) and an accent language (Sranan). [...] In Saramaccan it is the syllable that carries the pitch level [...], whereas in Sranan it is the word that carries a difference of pitch.
new_statements.citation: Voorhoeve, Jan. 1961. Le ton et la grammaire dans le Saramaccan. Word 17:146-163.
new_statements.locator: p. 146 (sec. 1 'Le but de cette etude' and footnote 2); PDF page 2
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the the Internet Archive T&F PDF; the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Le ton et la grammaire dans le Saramaccan', cover page cites word 17:2, 146-163, DOI..11659750). The quoted sentences are at the text layerand 60-64 (p. 146, sec. 1) and fn. 2 at lines 67-78, verbatim apart from stripped diacritics and scanned 'Ia' for 'la' (reader normalised to 'la'). Read secs. 1-3 and the conclusion: the paper treats Saramaccan as a two-level tone language (aigu/grave), syllabe = tone-bearing unit, tone sandhi and syntaxeme-final lowering, tonal word-structure constraints; no word-stress placement rule anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent|stress|intensit: only fn. 2'…
new_statements.relation_note: Supports the catalog's tonal coding of Saramaccan (two contrastive level tones, syllable as tone-bearing unit) and explicitly classes Saramaccan as a tone language as opposed to an accent language (Sranan). It is silent on the derived, foot-based stress placement that Rountree 1972 (existing statement) describes and on Good 2004's pitch accent/tone lexical split; nothing in it contradicts either.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Saramaccan is analysed as a tone language with two contrastive level tones (high 'aigu' and low 'grave'), every syllable bearing a tone; the paper then describes tone sandhi ('perturbation'), the phrase-final lowering that closes the 'syntaxeme', and tonal word-structure constraints (no low syllable between highs inside a one-morph word). Word stress/accent placement is never described; the only accent statements are the explicit typological contrast with Sranan ('langue a accent avec accent sur le mot', p. 156) and the remark that a handful of irregular reduplications (biibii, sakasaka, kasikaasi, kesikesi) follow Sranan word-accent formation and are taken to be Sranan loans.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 156: a small group of reduplications with a single high syllable 'suivent completement les principes de formation du mot dans le Sranan, langue a accent avec accent sur le mot' and are judged borrowed from Sranan; intensifier words (faan, gbolo, kololoo) have anomalous all-high tone structures with an extensible final syllable (pp. 151-152).
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern the Upper Suriname River variety of Saramaccan (Voorhoeve: 'Haut Surinam', material largely collected by A. Donicie; Glock: upper Suriname River, SIL fieldwork since 1968), the same variety as Rountree 1972 in the existing statement.

(2) The classification rests on a 2004 Lingua phonology article by the language's principal phonologist, not on a pedagogical or second-hand source; Glottolog's descriptive list offers nothing stronger on prosody except the 2012 De Gruyter grammar co-written by the same author (ch. 2 Prosodic phonology, pp. 30-62, paywalled). (3) Three open Good preprints downloaded now (2005, 2006, 2009) all restate the 2004 analysis: majority-class words carry one lexically contrastive accent realized as H tone, stress is predictable from the accent via trochaic footing, fully tone-specified words

sources.note: Lexicon is split: classes (i)-(iii) are fully tone-specified (H/L contrastive, minimal pairs) and show no stress effects; the majority class (iv) carries one lexically placed pitch accent (realized as H, contrastive position: bigí vs bígi), from which stress is derived by parsing into trochaic feet from the leftmost H TBU (primary stress near the left edge, alternating secondary). Rountree 1972b's weight/penult-of-foot rule is quoted on p. 14 and reinterpreted. This is the catalog's deciding source; the catalog quote is verbatim from it.

sources.quote: 'as discussed in Good (2004b:586-594), the former class of words [pitch-accented] exhibit effects which can be associated with stress while the latter [truly tonal] does not. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: The correlation between pitch accent and stress is not completely trivial—that is, it is not simply the case that the stressed syllable is the same as the syllable containing the vowel marked with a high tone. However, it is predictable and, as discussed in Good (2004:588–592), can be straightforwardly analyzed using an algorithm that (i) parses words marked for accent into trochaic feet based on the position of the lexically-specified accent mark and (ii) assigns stress to the leftmost trochaic foot (with the result that stress is always found near the beginning of the word even if accent is not).
sources.note: Cleanest one-sentence statement of the Good analysis, with stress-marked forms: ˈnáki, foˈló, ˈíngísi, siˈkífi, ˈmɔkisá, miˈnísíti, ˈafokáti, aˈlukutú; stress diagnostics are high-vowel syncope in unstressed syllables (mɔkisá → mɔksá) and emphatic lengthening in stressed ones (sákása → sá:kása).
